questions.stem: A study table shows marginal revenue $14 and marginal cost $14.

options.misconception: confuses with long-run
confuses "Output should be increased" with the correct "Output is at the profit-maximizing level"
names "Output should be decreased" where the rule requires "Output is at the profit-maximizing level"

options.text: Output is at the profit-maximizing level.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this what the marginal rule compares item is: MR equals MC at optimum. That is why "Output is at the profit-maximizing level" is right. The option "The firm should exit" (confuses with long-run) does not satisfy the rule.

questions.stem: A study group asks what portion of marginal cost is supply.

answer.exemplar: The portion of marginal cost that lies above minimum average variable cost.

questions.explanation: Only the portion above minimum AVC forms supply. A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost above the minimum of average variable cost. Supplying at any price above zero is the common error.

questions.stem: Market demand is 6000 units and efficient scale is 150 units.
questions.explanation: 6000 divided by 150 equals 40. Free entry drives economic profit to zero in the long run, so price settles at the minimum of average total cost under perfect competition. Assuming profit stays positive is the common mistake.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A study group asks what sustains a trigger strategy.

options.misconception: selects "Cheating gain outweighs future punishment" instead of "Future punishment outweighs cheating gain"
trigger requires punishment
would undermine trigger

questions.explanation: A trigger strategy deters cheating because the punishment that follows a deviation outweighs the immediate gain. Reversing the inequality removes the deterrent, no punishment makes the threat empty, and short horizons make future losses too small to matter.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The gain from a dominant strategy
questions.stem: Dominant payoff is $18 and alternative payoff is $11.
questions.explanation: 18 - 11 = 7. A dominant strategy yields at least as good a payoff as any other action regardless of what rivals do, so its gain is the payoff advantage across states. Comparing payoffs only in one state is the common mistake.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Marginal revenue from a demand elasticity
questions.stem: Price is $6 and elasticity is -2.
questions.explanation: MR = 6 times (1 - 1/2) = 3. Marginal revenue equals price times one plus the inverse of elasticity, so it sits below price when demand is elastic. Adding rather than adding the inverse elasticity is the common error.
